beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Nine times six. What if you don't know it yet?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: We'll use three moves: turn it, regroup it, or split it. Each keeps the total.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Start by splitting. Nine rows, six dots in each. This fence separates one column from five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Nine times one is nine. Nine times five is forty-five. Together, fifty-four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Slide the fence. Two columns and four columns: eighteen plus thirty-six. The same fifty-four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Slide again. Three and three: twenty-seven plus twenty-seven. Still fifty-four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Which cut gives you facts you know?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Five and one! I know nine times five, and one more column adds nine.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Exactly. One extra dot in every row means nine extra dots. Nothing was added or removed when the fence moved.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Multiplying each part, then adding, is the distributive property.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: This region is one part of the picture. How many squares are in region *A*?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Two rows of five. Ten squares.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. Count only that region's rows. If all twenty-five squares and those ten are known, the other region has fifteen.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is six times four: twenty-four dots. Turn the array a quarter turn.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four rows of six! Same twenty-four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Swapping the two numbers in a multiplication is the commutative property.

do.meaning: Swap the order; keep the product.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Turn back. Twenty-four shared into six equal rows gives four in each. So the multiplication also tells us a division fact.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Suppose you also know six times five is thirty. These two arrays have the same six rows.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Join them. Four and five make nine dots in every row.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Then six times nine is twenty-four plus thirty. Fifty-four!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Choose parts that make the whole nine, and multiply both parts by six.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Regrouping helps with groups inside groups. Four crates. Four bags in each crate. Three balls in each bag.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Count bags first. Four times four makes sixteen bags. Each holds three balls.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Or keep the crates. Four bags of three make twelve balls per crate.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four crates of twelve. Forty-eight again. Same balls, different grouping.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The curved marks, parentheses, show what to work out first. Changing the grouping is the associative property.

do.meaning: Change the grouping; keep the product.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Try four times two times two. Group the first two numbers: four times two makes eight pairs.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Group the last two: two times two makes four in each box. Four times four is sixteen.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Either way, use all three numbers. Regrouping changes which multiplication you do first.

do.text: Same numbers. Same order. New grouping.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Split for division, too. Share seventy-two dots equally among six trays. Split seventy-two into sixty and twelve.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Share sixty first. Ten on every tray.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Share the remaining twelve among the same six trays. Two more on every tray.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Ten plus two is twelve on each tray. So seventy-two divided by six is twelve.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Keep the same six trays for both loads. Check: six times twelve is seventy-two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A property names the change. Look at these two ways to group six times five times eight.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: The numbers stay in order. Only the parentheses move. That's regrouping, with multiplication.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Both equal two hundred forty. Match the change and the operation.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Swapping also works for addition. Four plus five, or five plus four. Same nine dots.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Regrouping works for addition, too. Two plus three first, then five. Or three plus five first, then two. Ten either way.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One more name: identity. Adding zero leaves five dots. Multiplying five by one leaves one copy of five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: For identity of addition, choose the plus zero equation. For multiplication, choose times one.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three moves. Turn changes the order. Regroup changes the grouping. Split multiplies the parts, then adds.

do.text: Turn it, regroup it, split it

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Nine times six? Forty-five plus nine. Fifty-four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: You never face a hard fact alone; turn it, regroup it, or split it.
